units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels is two things at once.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's a small, very old Belgian city that grew up on a muddy river.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And it's the main home of the European Union.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And those two things don't always look alike.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They really don't. In one walk you can go from a medieval guild square to a glass office tower full of EU officials.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Let's do the mud first.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The river is called the Senne.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The name of the city comes from an old word meaning a home in the marsh.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: People settled along that river, merchants on the road between Flanders and Cologne stopped here, and a market town grew.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: How old are we talking?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The date people usually give for the founding is around the year nine seventy-nine, when a Frankish nobleman called Charles moved the relics of a saint named Gudula to a chapel on an island in the river.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels celebrated its thousandth birthday in 1979.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Is that exactly true?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Historians say the story is probably tidier than the reality.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But it's the date that stuck.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, that's the old city. Then what?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Then centuries of other people's empires.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Burgundy, Spain, Austria, France, and the Netherlands, and then in 1830 a revolution, and Belgium becomes its own country with Brussels as the capital.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the second thing? The EU.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: After the Second World War, Belgium was one of the six countries that founded what became the European Union.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels ended up with the European Commission and the Council, and the Parliament does much of its work here too.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's why you'll see so many flags and so many languages.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Languages. That's the third thing.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The third thing. Brussels is officially bilingual, French and Dutch.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Every street sign has both. In daily life, French is spoken by most people, but you'll hear Dutch, English, and dozens of other languages.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Nearly four in ten residents hold a foreign passport.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So don't be surprised if somebody switches language mid-sentence.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Don't be surprised, and don't feel bad about starting with English.
